newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: IMF, World Bank Zambia programmes seen in jeopardy.
newsitem.headline: IMF, World Bank Zambia programmes seen in jeopardy.

text.p: A freeze on donor aid to Zambia has placed International Monetary Fund and World Bank programmes in jeopardy, a Standard Chartered Bank (Zambia) report released on Friday said.
The report said the suspension of balance of payment support by most western governments had made it difficult for Zambia to meet the economic benchmarks set by the institutions.
"On the strictly economic front, the September performance benchmarks set by the IMF have now assumed enormous importance," the report said.
"Not only is the disbursement of IMF funding under the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility loan on the line, but so is our World Bank lending and that of some bilateral donors," the report said.
It said Zambia's net international reserves - the key benchmark - was down to about three weeks import cover, against the three months recommended by donors.

"If the September benchmarks are to be met, the signs are that the exchange rate will weaken significantly from current levels (1,270 to the dollar) as the Bank of Zambia builds up its reserves, driving the kwacha down in the process.
"A year-end figure in the region of 1,450 to 1,500 to the dollar - a 15 percent devaluation from current levels - is likely," the report said.

A central bank official said the level of reserves was higher than the report indicated. "We have more than a month's worth in reserves, maybe six weeks worth," the central bank assistant director of information, Patrick Mulenga, told Reuters.
He declined to speculate on the implications of the low level of reserves on the World Bank and IMF programmes.
The Standard Chartered report predicted a worsening balance of payments situation for as long as the donor freeze on balance of payments support persisted and copper earnings remained low.

"In recent years, donor-balance of payments support has averaged $275 million annually, but this year the figure is unlikely to be more than half that - at best. With the available resources down to three weeks import cover, there is virtually no room to manoeuvre," it said.
Western governments, led by the U.S., have cut or frozen aid in response to new laws they say limit Zambians' choice of a president.
The laws ban second generation Zambians, and former presidents who ruled for two terms, from standing for president.
Both categories apply to former president Kenneth Kaunda, who heads the largest opposition party.
